data.name: Shemaiel
data.long_meaning: Derived from the Hebrew name Shammah, meaning 'god hears'. In the Bible, Shemaiel is a priest who prophesies against King Joash of Judah, reminding him of his duty to God.
data.spiritual_meaning: A name reminding the bearer of their duty to God and inspiring obedience.

in_hebrew.name: שמאאל
in_hebrew.meaning: שמעאל שמו של אלוהים או אלוהים שמע
in_hebrew.long_meaning: שמעאל הוא שם עברי שפירושו 'שמעאל' או 'אלוהים שמע'. הוא מורכב משתי מילים: 'שמע' שפירושו 'שמע' ו'אל' שפירושו 'אלוהים'. השם שמעאל מוזכר בתנ'ך כבן של אברהם ופילגש שלו, הגר. הוא נחשב לאב של שבט ערב.

in_greek.name: Σημαήλ
in_greek.meaning: Σημαήλ το όνομα του Θεού ή Θεός ακούει
in_greek.long_meaning: Σημαήλ είναι ένα εβραϊκό όνομα που σημαίνει 'το όνομα του Θεού' ή 'Θεός ακούει'. Είναι σύνθετο από δύο λέξεις: 'שמע' που σημαίνει 'ακούει' και 'אל' που σημαίνει 'Θεός'. Ο Σημαήλ αναφέρεται στην Αγία Γραφή ως γιος του Αβραάμ και της υπηρετούς του, Αγάρη. Θεωρείται ο πρόγονος του αραβικού έθνους.

in_latin.name: Shemail
in_latin.meaning: Shemail name of God or God hears
in_latin.long_meaning: Shemail is a Hebrew name meaning 'name of God' or 'God hears'. It is derived from two words: 'shama' meaning 'to hear' and 'el' meaning 'God'. Shemail is mentioned in the Bible as the son of Abraham and his concubine Hagar. He is considered the ancestor of the Arab people.

in_english.name: Shemaiel
in_english.meaning: God hears or name of God
in_english.long_meaning: Shemaiel is a Hebrew name that originated from the Bible, meaning 'God hears' or 'name of God'. It is derived from the Hebrew words 'shama', meaning 'to hear', and 'el', meaning 'God'. In the Bible, Shemaiel is the son of Abraham and his concubine Hagar, considered the ancestor of the Arab people. The name Shemaiel holds significant spiritual meaning, symbolizing divine connection and hearing. It is used across Christian cultures, signifying a strong bond with God.

data.cultural_impact: The name Shemaiel carries biblical roots, evoking a sense of history and can be seen as a connection to the Jewish and Middle Eastern cultures. It highlights the importance of religion and prophecy in shaping societal norms and establishes a connection to the rich traditions of the past.
data.spiritual_significance: The name Shemaiel is a powerful reminder of the belief that God is always listening and that our actions and faith are essential in maintaining a connection with the divine. It highlights the importance of spiritual introspection and the responsibility of individuals to live in accordance with the will of God, serving as a motivator for righteousness and obedience.

historical_references.reference: Shemaiel the Seer mentioned in the Old Testament Book of Zechariah (13:1-6). This prophecy speaks of a future time when two-thirds of the inhabitants of Jerusalem will be cut off and destroyed, and the remaining one-third will be saved. Shemaiel is identified as the one who will shepherd this remnant of Israel.
historical_references.context: The time of the Second Temple, during which the Jews were returning from the Babylonian exile to rebuild Jerusalem and the Temple.

historical_references.reference: Shemaiel, a Jewish leader mentioned in the New Testament Book of Acts (21:30), is accused of stirring up a riot against Paul in the Temple precincts.
historical_references.context: The time of the Apostles, during which Paul was on his third missionary journey.

modern_usage.modern_context: Shemaiel (שְׁמַיֵּאל in Hebrew) is a biblical name mentioned in the Book of Ezekiel. In modern times, the name Shemaiel has gained significance in Jewish studies and mysticism. It is commonly found in the contexts of Tanach study, Jewish mysticism, and biblical commentary. Shemaiel is often referenced in the works of various Jewish scholars, particularly those focusing on the mystical aspects of the Bible and Jewish tradition. On platforms like MyJewishLearning.com, Chabad.org, and JSTOR, you can find numerous articles, essays, and studies that delve into the meaning and significance of the name Shemaiel in Jewish thought and practice.

Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength." (Deuteronomy 6:4-5)
